summary:
ASTRA: Astronomical Satellite Tracking and Retrieval Architecture

ASTRA is a modular, web-based space engineering platform that brings spacecraft design, orbital infrastructure and planetary observation into one interactive, mission-driven experience. Instead of learning these topics from static diagrams or complex specialist tools, users build, validate and fly missions in 3D, together.

The platform combines three applications on a shared backend. The Orbital Space Station demonstrates docking, resupply and mission coordination. The Space Shuttle and Spacecraft Designer supports modular assembly, component replacement, engineering calculations and versioned configurations. The Planetary Scanning Satellite demonstrates observation workflows and data collection.

Up to three players join a mission room, coordinate in real time and complete missions: Earth Observation Satellite deployment, Space Station resupply and a Lunar landing. The server validates critical outcomes, so results cannot be faked by a client, and players can reconnect after a dropout.

ASTRA makes space engineering approachable, rewards experimentation, and is built to grow with new spacecraft, environments and missions. It is developed by Dhananjaya N., Muzamill Pasha and Chandan G. using AI-assisted tools and GitHub collaboration, and is designed for both laptop and mobile browsers.
details:
ASTRA is a web-based space engineering platform made of three connected applications: an Orbital Space Station, a Spacecraft Designer, and a Planetary Scanning Satellite. Players join a mission room and work together to complete missions.

My module is the Orbital Mission Simulator. Three players fly one spacecraft in real-time 3D under real orbital physics (gravity, thrust, fuel burn and changing mass), with time warp so full orbits can be played. Each player has a role: Flight controls thrust and rotation, Engineering manages the engine and fuel, and Science deploys the satellite and runs data collection. The mission is Earth Observation Satellite Deployment: raise a 300 km orbit to a circular 500 km orbit with two burns, deploy the satellite and transmit the data.

The server runs the simulation. Clients send only inputs, and the server checks each one by role and mission phase, then decides fuel, phase changes, deployment success and score. Results are saved to a PostgreSQL database.

What are the benefits?

It teaches how orbits work, for example that you burn twice, and why the opposite side of an orbit rises when you burn prograde, through hands-on play instead of formulas. A live guide shows what to do next with real numbers. Teamwork is required, since no single player can complete the mission alone.

What is the intended impact?

To make space engineering approachable for students and enthusiasts, to encourage experimentation, and to provide a modular base that can take new spacecraft, planets and missions.

Tools, languages and software

  • Languages: TypeScript, JavaScript, SQL, HTML and CSS.
  • Frontend: React, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Zustand, Three.js with React Three Fiber and Drei.
  • Backend: Node.js, Express, Socket.IO, Zod validation, JWT guest login.
  • Database: PostgreSQL on Neon, with Prisma.
  • Testing: Vitest, including a scripted full-mission simulation and a three-bot multiplayer test.
  • Hosting: Vercel, Render and Neon
  • Development: Google Antigravity and Google AI Studio for AI-assisted coding, and GitHub for collaboration.
  • Hardware: standard laptops and any modern browser; no special hardware.

How is it creative?

It treats orbital mechanics as a cooperative game. Role-based crew play, a server-authoritative simulation, a split HUD with a live mission guide, cinematic camera shots and astronaut conversation captions turn a physics lesson into a shared mission. The physics is real: SI units, velocity Verlet integration and tested burn values, with the first burn about 57 m/s and the total about 114 m/s.

What factors did the team consider?

  • Accuracy: unit tests check the physics, and a headless simulation checks the full mission against hand-calculated numbers.
  • Fair play: the server validates all critical outcomes, so a client can’t fake a result.
  • Reliability: reconnection support, and a “server waking up” state for free hosting.
  • Accessibility: a guided mission panel and a help overlay for new players.
  • Performance: a floating-origin renderer, a quality toggle and capped pixel ratio for mid-range laptops.
  • Scope and independence: each team member built their module independently, with a shared architecture for future integration.
  • Credits: imagery sources and a statement that the project is independent and not affiliated with NASA.
